seo_title: Champ: Lake Champlain's monster and the Mansi photo
seo_desc: Lake Champlain's Champ from the 1819 serpent report to Sandra Mansi's 1977 photo, the 2005 video and what the image analysts actually concluded.
summary: America's Loch Ness, from Mohawk giant-snake stories and an 1819 sea serpent report to Sandra Mansi's photo and the 2005 fishermen's video.
body: Champ is the monster of Lake Champlain, the long lake shared by New York, Vermont and a corner of Quebec. People have been seeing something in it for a long time and there are more than 300 reported sightings, which is a lot even for a lake this size.

The story runs from Mohawk accounts of giant snakes through an 1819 newspaper report of a 187 ft serpent, a 1883 sheriff who got a close look, and P.T. Barnum offering money for a carcass. The modern version rests on one photograph from 1977 and one video from 2005.
I think something is out there being misread, and the Mansi photo is the reason this story has lasted. It's a good picture (until you ask where the negative went).

sections.h: The lake and the giant snakes
p: Lake Champlain is about 200 km long (125 miles) and more than 120 m deep in places, plenty of water to keep a story alive. The Mohawk told of Onyare'kowa, giant serpents in the water, and those Iroquois stories are the oldest layer under everything else. The Abenaki name that shows up in local retellings is Tatoskok.

French cartographer Samuel de Champlain, whose name the lake carries, is often called the first European to see the monster in 1609. That claim comes from a magazine article in 1970, not from anything he wrote. What he did write about is a fish the locals called chaoufarou, up to 3 m long, with a snout, a double row of sharp teeth and scales a dagger couldn't pierce. A 1878 translation of his journals works out that chaoufarou means gar, the longnose gar that still lives in the lake. So the founding sighting is a fish, which is honestly how a lot of these start.

In 1819 the Plattsburgh Republican ran a piece called Cape Ann Serpent on Lake Champlain, in which a Captain Crum said he saw a serpent roughly 57 m long (187 ft) about 180 m away. At that distance he still managed to note three teeth, a belt of red around its neck, a white star on its forehead, and eyes the colour of peeled onions, plus two sturgeon and a bill-fish following it. I'd like to meet the man who can count teeth at 180 m.

Sheriff Nathan Mooney did better in 1883. He said the thing came within about 100 m of him and was 25 to 30 ft long, close enough that he could see round white spots inside its mouth. A sheriff with a description that specific is worth more than a sea captain's 57 m snake, and Mooney's report brought a wave of other witnesses out of the woodwork.
P.T. Barnum got involved twice, offering a reward for a carcass in 1873 and again in 1887. He never had to pay it (the man made a career out of not paying out on lake monsters).

Sandra Mansi was on vacation with her family near St. Albans, Vermont in July 1977 when she took a photo of what looks like a head and neck coming out of the water. It's the best-known monster photo in North America after the Loch Ness one, partly because it looks like a living thing.

The problems start when you ask about the place and the film. The bay where she said she took it is no deeper than about 4 m, which is not enough water for a big animal to swim in, let alone hide in, as Joe Nickell has pointed out. The object could be a log or a tree trunk rolling up in the water. And when the photo went to Philip Reines, a nautical expert at SUNY Plattsburgh, he found that the two things he needed were gone, because Mansi had thrown away the negative and couldn't find the spot again. With no negative and no location you can't work out the size of the thing, how far away it was, or even prove it was taken on Champlain. Reines couldn't authenticate it, and Robert Bartholomew's book on the case goes through the rest of the holes.
P.T. Barnum got involved twice, offering a reward for a carcass in 1873 and again in 1887. He never had to pay it, which tells you how the carcass market was going.

In the summer of 2005 two fishermen, Dick Affolter and his stepson Pete Bodette, filmed something in the lake that can be read as a head and neck with an open mouth, or as a fish, or as an eel. Two retired FBI forensic image analysts looked at the tape and said it seemed authentic and unmanipulated, and then one of them added that he couldn't actually see an animal or any object on the surface in it. That's about as close as this story gets to a professional opinion, and it doesn't land where believers want.

Two years earlier a research group recorded sounds in the lake for a Discovery Channel programme and described them as similar to beluga whales or dolphins, neither of which lives in Champlain. The published paper settled on some form of echolocation, which none of the lake's known animals do. Nobody has explained where the noise came from.

In 2024 the people making a film called Lucy and the Lake Monster found something on their drone footage swimming under the surface in Bulwagga Bay, behind a boat, apparently longer than the boat. It's the newest entry in the file and it hasn't been tested yet.

Port Henry, New York keeps a roadside board of sightings, and Burlington and Plattsburgh both sell the monster on T-shirts and signs, so the tourism side is easy to find. The lake is the real draw, especially the narrow middle section between the New York and Vermont shores where most reports come from.
Go early, go quiet, and take two photos of anything strange, one of the thing and one of where you were standing (the Mansi case would have been closed on day one with that habit).

faq.a: There's no body, and the two best pieces of evidence both have holes. The Mansi photo can't be verified because the negative and the location are gone, and the 2005 video was called unmanipulated by FBI image analysts who also said they couldn't see an animal in it. Something has been seen in that lake many times, and misread fish, logs and wakes explain a lot of it.

faq.q: What is Champ called in Native stories?
faq.a: The Mohawk told of Onyare'kowa, giant serpents in the water, and the Iroquois accounts of big snakes in that country are older than any settler report. Local retellings also use the Abenaki name Tatoskok.

faq.q: Where was the Mansi photo taken?
faq.a: Sandra Mansi said she took it near St. Albans, Vermont in July 1977. She couldn't find the exact spot afterwards, which matters because the bay she described is only about 4 m deep, too shallow for a large animal to hide in.

faq.q: Did Samuel de Champlain see Champ?
faq.a: No evidence says he did. The claim comes from a 1970 magazine article, and what Champlain actually wrote about was a large gar fish with a double row of teeth, which he saw and described in his journals.

The best-known footage is the 2005 video by Dick Affolter and Pete Bodette, which two retired FBI image analysts said looked unmanipulated, though one said he couldn't see an animal in it. A 2024 drone shot from the film Lucy and the Lake Monster is the newest piece of footage and hasn't been examined.

faq.q: How many Champ sightings are there?
faq.a: More than 300 reported sightings over about two centuries, which is a large number for one lake and part of why the story survives. Most come from the narrow middle of the lake between the New York and Vermont shores.
